DPDP ACT · RTI · SUPREME COURT Privacy vs. the right to know: the DPDP Act in court On 17 November, the Supreme Court hears the challenges to India's data protection law again. Beyond the publishers' plea, the case asks whether a privacy law has weakened RTI, allowed unchecked state access to data, and left the regulator under executive control. BEYOND RTI Five more provisions under challenge 1 s. 17 exemptions: the State can exempt its agencies, allegedly without safeguards or review. 2 s. 36 with Rule 23(2): the Centre can demand data from any fiduciary, and the person may not be told. 3 s. 18 with Rule 17: Board members chosen by an executive- led committee; independence questioned. 4 s. 33(1): penalties for a "significant" breach, a term the Act doesn't define. 5 No journalism exemption: the publishers' plea, on consent and erasure. TA K E AWAY Privacy should protect people, not shield power. A data protection law should stop misuse of personal data. It shouldn't stop citizens from checking how public money and public power are used. The Supreme Court now has to draw that line. Adv.
